extracted.intended_audience: academic physicians, surgical trainees, and early-career peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing constructive, ethical, and methodologically sound peer reviews of medical/scientific manuscripts, covering review structure, study-design and statistical appraisal, ethical considerations, and professional development as a reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-blind review model
rubrics_metrics.description: In the single-blind model, the identities of the reviewers are not revealed to the authors, but the authors' identities are revealed to the reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers can provide honest feedback while ensuring no conflicts of interest with the authors or institutions; however, authors are not protected from reviewers' implicit or explicit biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind review model
rubrics_metrics.description: In the double-blind model, neither the reviewers nor authors are aware of the others’ identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents believe it mitigates biases of both parties, but evidence for improved review quality is lacking and true blinding may fail (authors identifiable by style, subject matter, or self-citation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open review model
rubrics_metrics.description: In the open model of peer review, the authors and the reviewers are aware of the others’ identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages respectful feedback and constructive criticism; may discourage honest criticism due to fear of retribution and make it harder to find reviewers, though trials show no difference in quality versus blinded reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepublication (preprint) review model
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprint manuscripts and dynamic reviews available online during development; manuscripts can later be submitted to a journal for formal review and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows early feedback and iterative improvement prior to formal submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication peer review allows for comments, discussion, and formal reviews posted online after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can provide a wide range of perspectives to improve future work and shape subsequent versions if authors apply feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent review services
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviews are provided independent of a particular journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews are portable and can be reliably verified by journals interested in a submission (useful for cascading/re-use of reviews).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative review model
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers work directly with authors on article revisions toward a final product suitable for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blurs reviewer/author roles but can accelerate improvement toward publication-ready work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with common study designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer should be familiar with study design, since it dictates data quality, appropriate analysis, and generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand strengths/weaknesses of case reports/case series, cross-sectional, cohort, case-control, ecological, interventional (randomized and nonrandomized), qualitative studies; use design-appropriate checklists and evaluate whether conclusions match design limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational study appraisal (use STROBE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational studies include descriptive (case reports/series) and analytic (cross-sectional, cohort, case-control) types; findings may not be generalizable and are hypothesis-generating in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use STROBE checklist to ensure all necessary components are present; check for confounding, appropriate comparison groups, and limits to causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interventional study appraisal (use CONSORT/TREND)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventional studies include nonrandomized trials, randomized controlled trials (gold standard), pre–post designs, and trials without concurrent controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CONSORT for randomized trials and TREND for nonrandomized designs; assess randomization, control groups, follow-up, and whether the design supports the authors' claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative study appraisal (use COREQ/SRQR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative research explores perspectives and experiences rather than testing hypotheses and is context-dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rationale, methodology, sampling, data collection, personnel, and interpretation; ensure methods are described sufficiently and results move beyond description to interpretation; consult COREQ and SRQR reporting checklists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-chapter review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical book chapters aim to provide general overviews or in-depth reviews of topics and should be authored and reviewed by subject-matter experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess relevance to chapter topic, usefulness to the field, comprehensiveness of literature review, clarity of conclusions supported by references or expertise, logical organization, and whether tables/figures add value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer statistical competency
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must be proficient in study design, basic descriptive and comparative statistics, and measures of association and know when to call a statistician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note if analyses require complex statistical review and recommend confidential editor-requested statistician review when appropriate; check that data organization logically guides readers to authors' conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate descriptive statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must determine whether data are normally distributed; mean is appropriate for normally distributed continuous data with few outliers, median for skewed distributions; mode useful for categorical variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure authors choose correct measures of central tendency and present data effectively in tables/figures; reviewers should highlight unnecessary data and suggest emphasis on salient results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate comparative statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative tests must match variable types and distributions (e.g., t-test for means, ANOVA for multiple groups, chi-square or Fisher's exact for categorical variables, Kaplan–Meier/log-rank for time-to-event).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm right tests used given distribution and variable type; advise on matched-pair vs independent-sample tests and appropriate use of Fisher vs chi-square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivariable analysis appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying associations, multivariable analyses (odds ratios, hazard ratios, relative risk) should be performed as appropriate and covariates should be clearly reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check which covariates were included, how they were chosen, whether relevant covariates were excluded, and caution against inappropriate causal language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured review strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a systematic way to approach a review (examples: abstract→figures→manuscript or read top-to-bottom) and clearly delineate major vs minor points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the review so that critical issues required for revision are separated from minor stylistic comments; follow a consistent checklist (Table 3) to ensure coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before accepting review (screening criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before accepting an invitation, confirm sufficient subject-matter expertise, ability to meet the deadline, and absence of personal or financial conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decline or recuse if lacking expertise, if unable to finish timely, or if COIs are present; consider mentoring arrangements requiring editor/mentor permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide actionable, constructive feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should provide constructive feedback in a respectful manner such that manuscript quality is improved and should provide actionable items even if the manuscript will be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus comments on how to improve the work; give specific suggestions rather than only criticisms, and separate tone for authors vs confidential comments to editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on big-picture scientific quality over grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should appraise scientific quality and value of the literature rather than focusing on grammatical/editorial details, unless poor grammar makes the manuscript unreadable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize study validity, methods, results interpretation, and impact; reserve micro-editing comments for truly problematic prose or journal copyediting stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the journal's scope and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be familiar with the journal's scope, readership, and preferred manuscript and review formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm manuscript fits journal aims and structured abstract/formatting requirements; tailor comments to expected audience and journal conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess novelty and potential impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider potential impact and novelty of the manuscript: does it address an important topic, add to existing literature, pave way for future studies, or influence clinical practice?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform a brief literature check to ensure prior work is acknowledged and to contextualize novelty; comment on whether the work fills a gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract should grab the reader’s attention, accurately summarize the paper and main conclusions, and fit the journal’s format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure abstract reflects key results and potential impact; check for structured abstract requirements and length limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction should logically explain the reason for the study and clearly state primary and secondary aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify background sets up the research question, gaps in knowledge are identified, and aims are explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods appraisal (ethical and reporting standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods should include IRB approval statement (where appropriate), reference to appropriate reporting guidelines, clear inclusion/exclusion criteria, and use of appropriate statistical tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm adherence to reporting guidelines (e.g., STROBE/CONSORT/TREND/COREQ), evaluate population selection for generalizability and bias, and request missing methodological details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Results should be well organized by population and/or topic, include pertinent demographic characteristics, and not merely restate tables/figures in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that tables and figures have clear titles and legends, avoid excessive overlap between text and displays, and ensure results are presented clearly for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion should succinctly summarize the most important results, place them in the context of pertinent and up-to-date literature, state how results are significant, and include appropriate limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for realistic interpretation of findings, appropriate claims about significance, balanced consideration of strengths/weaknesses, and suggestions for future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes reporting clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: One primary outcome should be clearly defined with secondary outcomes listed separately; the reviewer should note how outcomes are reported (continuous vs categorical) and choose appropriate analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure primary outcome is prespecified and analyses align to outcome types; question multiple primary outcomes or outcome-switching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography and citation quality
rubrics_metrics.description: References should be appropriate in number, quality, and range, including pertinent and recent literature; references should be complete and accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest additional relevant citations where appropriate but avoid recommending the reviewer’s own work; evaluate any outlying or questionable references for relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation and confidential comments to editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear recommendation regarding acceptance (accept, minor revisions, major revisions, reject) and compose a brief confidential comment for the editor explaining and justifying the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidential comments should not simply repeat comments to authors but highlight critical concerns, justification for recommendation, and potential need for statistician evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical responsibilities and COI management
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must be aware of ethical issues including conflicts of interest, expertise limits, timely submission, and confidentiality; COPE guidelines apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recuse when COIs exist or expertise is inadequate; disclose financial and nonfinancial COIs; respect confidentiality and follow journal-specific ethical policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling suspected misconduct or ethical concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewer is concerned about possible ethical violations (plagiarism, problematic study design, undisclosed COIs, data issues), they should address concerns directly with the handling editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise issues in the 'comments to editor' portion rather than in author-facing comments; many journals use plagiarism-detection software but reviewers should flag other concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal-level transparency and diversity expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should disclose financial and nonfinancial COIs for editors/reviewers and promote diversity among editors, editorial boards, and peer reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity (gender, race/ethnicity, career experience, geography, etc.) strengthens publication processes and reduces publication bias; reviewers should advocate for transparency where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reporting checklists and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should use established reporting guidelines appropriate to the study type (STROBE, CONSORT, TREND, COREQ, SRQR, SCARE etc.) to evaluate manuscript completeness and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify missing checklist components and request authors supply them prior to publication to promote rigorous reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer development: training and mentorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal educational programs and mentored review opportunities improve review quality; new reviewers should seek mentorship or peer-review academies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentored reviews require mentor permission from the handling editor and active mentor involvement in writing/editing the final review; participation can lead to editorial leadership opportunities.
